Series::extract_put_¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::extract_put_(pluss::RangeView<ExtractSpec> specs, const Series& values) -> Series&

What It Does¶

Writes into the current Series through the full selector language, mutates in place, and returns the same handle.

This is the broadest selector-based write surface on Series. If traverse_put_() is the strict method that only accepts selectors that stay view-representable, extract_put_() is the method that says “accept the richer selector language and materialize destination positions when necessary.”

That distinction matters in practice. This surface accepts things like:

  • reverse slices

  • bool masks

  • integer index Series

  • mixed selectors that cannot stay a plain view

The most useful mental model is simple:

  • extract() chooses values to read

  • extract_put_() chooses positions to write

Parameters¶

specs (pluss::RangeView<ExtractSpec>)

The destination selector.

This method accepts the same broad selector family taught on extract(), including:

  • scalar integer indices

  • bounded or unbounded slices

  • negative-step slices

  • SliceAll()

  • Ellipsis()

  • NewAxis()

  • bool mask Series

  • integer index Series

Write-side details are important here:

  • scalar indices consume an existing axis and narrow the addressed region

  • slices keep an axis and choose positions on it

  • Ellipsis() expands to however many identity slices are required

  • NewAxis() is accepted for selector compatibility, but it does not create a new writable axis

  • advanced selectors are materialized into explicit destination positions

values (const Series&)

The source values to assign into the selected destination positions.

Two cardinality rules apply:

  • if values.numel() == 1, the scalar source broadcasts across the entire selection

  • otherwise values.numel() must exactly match the number of selected destination elements

For non-scalar writes, matching is by selected element count. The original shape of values does not need to mirror the destination shape as long as the write cardinality is correct.

Returns¶

Series& The same Series, after mutation.

Examples¶

Example 1. Shared setup. Start from a simple 3 x 4 grid.

auto grid = pluss::make_series({
    {10.0, 11.0, 12.0, 13.0},
    {20.0, 21.0, 22.0, 23.0},
    {30.0, 31.0, 32.0, 33.0},
});

std::cout << grid;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=12, contiguous=true)
data=[[10, 11, 12, 13],
  [20, 21, 22, 23],
  [30, 31, 32, 33]]

Example 2. A scalar source broadcasts across every selected destination.

grid.extract_put_(
    {pluss::Slicing::SliceAll(), std::int64_t{1}},
    pluss::make_series(-1.0));

std::cout << grid;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=12, contiguous=true)
data=[[10, -1, 12, 13],
  [20, -1, 22, 23],
  [30, -1, 32, 33]]

Example 3. Reverse slices are legal here, so write order follows the selector’s logical visitation order.

grid.extract_put_(
    {std::int64_t{1}, pluss::Slicing::SliceRange(-1, pluss::Slicing::Slice::kUnbounded, -2)},
    pluss::make_series({90.0, 70.0}));

std::cout << grid;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=12, contiguous=true)
data=[[10, -1, 12, 13],
  [20, 70, 22, 90],
  [30, -1, 32, 33]]

The selector visits row 1, columns 3 then 1, so 90 lands in column 3 and 70 lands in column 1.

Example 4. NewAxis() is accepted for selector compatibility, but it does not create a new writable destination dimension.

grid.extract_put_(
    {pluss::Slicing::NewAxis(), pluss::Slicing::SliceAll(), std::int64_t{0}},
    pluss::make_series({100.0, 200.0, 300.0}));

std::cout << grid;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=12, contiguous=true)
data=[[100, -1, 12, 13],
  [200, 70, 22, 90],
  [300, -1, 32, 33]]

Semantically, this is still just “write column 0 for every row.”

Example 5. Bool masks are legal here because extract_put_() is allowed to materialize destination positions.

auto row_mask = pluss::make_series({true, false, true});

grid.extract_put_(
    {row_mask, pluss::Slicing::SliceAll()},
    pluss::make_series(0.0));

std::cout << grid;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=12, contiguous=true)
data=[[0, 0, 0, 0],
  [200, 70, 22, 90],
  [0, 0, 0, 0]]

Example 6. Integer index Series selectors can target explicit rows in the same write family.

auto picked_rows = pluss::make_series({2LL, 0LL});

grid.extract_put_(
    {picked_rows, pluss::Slicing::SliceAll()},
    pluss::make_series({
        {3000.0, 3001.0, 3002.0, 3003.0},
        {1000.0, 1001.0, 1002.0, 1003.0},
    }));

std::cout << grid;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=12, contiguous=true)
data=[[1000, 1001, 1002, 1003],
  [200, 70, 22, 90],
  [3000, 3001, 3002, 3003]]

Example 7. Ellipsis() also works on the write side and expands to the missing identity slices before the final write.

grid.extract_put_(
    {pluss::Slicing::Ellipsis(), std::int64_t{2}},
    pluss::make_series({12.5, 22.5, 32.5}));

std::cout << grid;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=12, contiguous=true)
data=[[1000, 1001, 12.5, 1003],
  [200, 70, 22.5, 90],
  [3000, 3001, 32.5, 3003]]

Example 8. Non-scalar sources must match the selected element count exactly.

try {
  grid.extract_put_(
      {std::int64_t{0}, pluss::Slicing::SliceRange(0, 4, 2)},
      pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}));
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

Series::extract_put_: source must be scalar or match selected element count

Example 9. Invalid slice step values fail before any write happens.

try {
  grid.extract_put_(
      {pluss::Slicing::SliceAll(), pluss::Slicing::SliceRange(0, 4, 0)},
      pluss::make_series(0.0));
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

Series::extract: step cannot be 0

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • NewAxis() is accepted, but it does not create a new writable destination axis.

  • Reverse slices are legal here, so source values follow selector visit order, not sorted position order.

  • Bool masks and integer index selectors are allowed because this method is willing to materialize explicit destination positions.

  • A zero slice step fails during selector normalization before any write occurs.

  • The selection count, not the visible destination shape, is what governs whether a non-scalar source is valid.

Summary¶

Reach for extract_put_() when you want the richest selector-language write surface on Series. It is the right method for masks, reverse slices, Ellipsis(), and advanced integer selectors. If you later realize your selector could have stayed a plain view all along, then traverse_put_() is the stricter sibling.

See Also¶

  • Series::traverse_put_: stricter in-place selector writes.

  • Series::extract: read-side counterpart.
